What kind of glass aquarium is this?
This is Victoria Sergeyevna's order, chef.
Why do we need this transparent wall?
It is needed to attract new guests.
This is a trendy open kitchen format.
Cooks should not be in an arena!
Guests love watching the cooking process.
They will see our every step.
On the other hand, there will be more patrons in the restaurant.
I am not a clown in a circus, Max.
Victoria Sergeyevna has already decided everything herself.
I will go talk to her right now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'aquarium' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Это что ещё за стеклянный аквариум?
examples.trans: What kind of glass aquarium is this?

examples.text: В центре зала стоит большой аквариум с рыбой.
examples.trans: A large aquarium with fish stands in the center of the hall.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'arena, stage' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Повара не должны быть на арене!
examples.trans: Cooks should not be in an arena!
Citizen Anikeev, you are under arrest.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'more'.
Secondary conversational sense ('bigger') (comparative of большой) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We need to do even more.
I don't need any more.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to see', forming an aspectual pair with 'увидеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = see?') (drawing attention) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

examples.text: Ты видишь, сколько гостей сегодня вечером сидит в зале?
examples.trans: Do you see how many guests are sitting in the hall tonight?

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.
You have visitors!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'cooking, food preparation' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Гости любят смотреть на процесс готовки.
examples.trans: Guests love watching the cooking process.
Right, I'm ready!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have to work.
Greed should be moderate.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: in threats: ты ещё увидишь = you'll see
Secondary conversational sense ('still, yet') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('even (with comparatives)') (ещё больше = even more) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: adds emphasis to the word before it

examples.trans: But you've still got some.
But I know.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

зато.gloss: but on the other hand, to make up for it

meanings.en: but on the other hand, at least
meanings.note: introduces a compensating positive fact

examples.text: Четыре по алгебре, зато по физкультуре пятёрка.
examples.trans: A four in algebra, but a five in gym.
The flat is small, but at least it's in the centre.

examples.text: Ничего страшного. Сейчас зато аппетит нагуляем.
examples.trans: No big deal. At least we'll walk up an appetite now.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'what for'.

examples.trans: What have you come for?
What's that for?
Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: Every day.
Every person.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'clown', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
an insult: someone who isn't serious

examples.trans: A clown works at the circus.
Don't be a clown!

examples.text: Хватит строить из себя смешного клоуна перед всей кухней.
examples.trans: Stop making a funny clown of yourself in front of the whole kitchen.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We're sitting in the kitchen.
Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to love, to like', paired with 'полюбить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to like') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
Do you like gum?

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: in 'рабочее место' = workplace, job
Secondary conversational sense ('post, position') (на его место = in his place) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: This is my seat.
It's a nice place here.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('fashionable, trendy, stylish').

examples.trans: This is a trendy open kitchen format.

examples.text: Это очень модный формат открытой кухни в Москве.
examples.trans: This is a very trendy open-kitchen format in Moscow.

examples.text: Нагиев пришёл в ресторан в новом модном костюме.
examples.trans: Nagiyev came to the restaurant in a new fashionable suit.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.trans: A new house.
I need a new job.

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: short form 'нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны' + dative: 'мне нужна работа' = I need a job

examples.trans: I need a job too.
Do you need a pen?
He needs money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: She's a lecturer.
I haven't heard of her.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: They are building a centre.
History will punish them.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to stay', forming an aspectual pair with 'остаться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: The advance stays with us.
I'm staying at home.
And the advance stays with us.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'крытый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('open, unclosed').

examples.trans: This is a trendy open kitchen format.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: There is this English chef.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.en: to have a talk, to speak (with someone)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'говорить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a talk', forming an aspectual pair with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: Talk to him.
We need to talk.

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: May I go?
Let's go home.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'full' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('complete, total, utter') (полный кошмар = a total nightmare) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: This is a total nightmare!

examples.text: На столе стоял полный стакан воды.
examples.trans: A full glass of water stood on the table.

examples.text: Ну что я тебе скажу, Аркаша? Это полный кошмар!
examples.trans: Well, what can I tell you, Arkasha? This is a total nightmare!

meanings.note: по порядку = in order; всё в порядке = everything is fine

examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

examples.text: Теперь давай всё по порядку. Скажи мне, сколько ты им должна?
examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order. Tell me, how much do you owe them?

meanings.note: person visiting a person, place, or institution

examples.trans: A visitor was sitting in the reception room.

examples.text: Это журнал посетителей мэрии из полицейских вещдоков.
examples.trans: This is the mayor's visitor log from police evidence.

examples.text: Зато в ресторане станет больше посетителей.
examples.trans: On the other hand, there will be more patrons in the restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'влечение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'attraction, engagement' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Она нужна для привлечения новых гостей.
examples.trans: It is needed to attract new guests.

examples.text: Эта яркая вывеска нужна для привлечения новых гостей с улицы.
examples.trans: This bright sign is needed for attracting new guests from the street.

examples.text: Вика придумала отличную акцию для привлечения постоянных клиентов.
examples.trans: Vika came up with a great promotion to attract regular clients.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'зрачный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('transparent, clear').

examples.trans: Why do we need this transparent wall?

examples.text: Мне сказали, что выборы должны пройти честно. Честно и прозрачно!
examples.trans: They told me that the election must be conducted honestly. Honestly and transparently!

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'цесс'). Common masculine noun meaning 'process, trial' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('legal trial') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And so the process stalled.
It is a long process.

examples.text: Ну и процесс остановился. Да арестовывать его надо, товарищ генерал!
examples.trans: And so the process stalled. We just need to arrest him, Comrade General!

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'поряжение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'order, instruction, directive' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Victoria Sergeyevna's order, chef.

examples.text: Это прямое распоряжение Виктории Сергеевны, шеф.
examples.trans: This is a direct instruction from Viktoriya Sergeyevna, Chef.

examples.text: Без личного распоряжения шефа никто не меняет рецепты блюд.
examples.trans: Without a personal directive from the chef, no one changes the dish recipes.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: + infinitive: решил стать = decided to become
Secondary conversational sense ('to solve') (решить задачу) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The court has decided.
I've decided.

examples.text: Суд решил: домашний арест по месту прописки.
examples.trans: The court has decided: house arrest at his registered address.

meanings.note: + instrumental; со before some consonant clusters: со всеми

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: I'll do it myself.
He knows himself.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вященный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('sacred, holy').

examples.trans: A sacred book.
Save the sacred book quickly!
The kitchen must remain a sacred place.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look', forming an aspectual pair with 'посмотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch') (TV, a film) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: + instrumental: стал сентиментальным
Secondary conversational sense ('to start (doing)') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: He became mayor.
You've changed.

examples.text: Ты слишком сентиментальным стал. А лидер должен быть жёстким.
examples.trans: You've become too sentimental. And a leader has to be tough.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'теклянный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('glass, glassy').

examples.text: Это что ещё за стеклянный аквариум?
examples.trans: What kind of glass aquarium is this?

examples.text: Это что ещё за странный стеклянный аквариум посреди кухни?
examples.trans: What kind of strange glass aquarium is this in the middle of the kitchen?

examples.text: Поставь свежие цветы в высокую стеклянную вазу на бар.
examples.trans: Put the fresh flowers into the tall glass vase on the bar.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'wall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: This is an old wall.
The picture is on the wall.

examples.text: Не надо врать. Стену монастыря сносят!
examples.trans: Don't lie. They're pulling down the monastery wall!

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
Dad is already home.
I'm already home.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'format, layout' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a trendy open kitchen format.
There's just one small formality.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'circus', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('farce, a ridiculous situation') (colloquial: цирк какой-то!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We're going to the circus.
What a circus!
What a circus.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: movement by foot or figurative action

examples.text: Надо следить за каждым шагом соперника.
examples.trans: We must monitor every step of the rival.
He took a step forward.

examples.text: Надо следить за каждым шагом кандидата.
examples.trans: We must monitor every step of the candidate.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.
